text: Equalize pressure across the DHSV, then reopen it through its hydraulic control line (corrective operating procedure).
why: Restores production quickly without a rig; the thesis notes timely detection allows reopening by corrective procedures.

text: Keep the well closed and schedule a DHSV inspection / workover.
why: Safest for the well barrier but loses production for days and may need a rig (> US$500k/day).

text: Force the DHSV open by raising control-line pressure without equalizing.
why: Fast, but can damage the valve and compromise a safety barrier.

text: Confirm with a fluid sample, then adjust choke / gas-lift to the new operating point.
why: Cheap and quick; keeps the well flowing with the heavier fluid.

text: Inform the reservoir team; review water injection and plan water shut-off.
why: Tackles the cause (water breakthrough) but takes time and money.

text: Continue unchanged and only monitor.
why: No cost now, but flow-assurance and processing problems may grow.

text: Choke back the production choke to stabilise the flow.
why: Classic mitigation: more back-pressure suppresses the slug cycle, at the price of some production.

text: Increase gas-lift injection to lighten the riser column.
why: Keeps more production but uses more gas and may not remove slugging.

text: Switch on active (feedback) slug control on the production choke.
why: Automatic choke control removes slugging with little production loss.

text: Ignore it and keep producing at full rate.
why: No production loss now, but repeated slugs stress and can damage equipment.

text: Watch closely and make a small choke adjustment to restore stable flow.
why: Instability can evolve into severe slugging, so act early but gently.

text: Adjust the gas-lift rate to a more stable operating point.
why: Changes the gas–liquid balance that drives the disturbances.

text: Change the operating point (open choke / increase gas lift) to keep natural flow.
why: The thesis: early detection lets operators change the operating point before flow is lost.

not_when.reason: Natural flow is already being lost; changing the operating point is no longer enough on its own.

text: Run a well test and update the reservoir model.
why: Confirms the cause before spending on interventions.

text: Plan a stimulation or artificial-lift intervention.
why: Long-term fix; needs intervention vessel or rig.

text: Check the production choke and restore it to its set-point.
why: The thesis: the choke is usually manual, so unwanted closures can be undone quickly.

text: Inspect the choke actuator / control system for faults.
why: Prevents the restriction from happening again.

text: Inject scale inhibitor upstream of the choke.
why: The thesis names scale-inhibitor injection as the appropriate action.

text: Dissolve the deposits with a chemical (acid) wash.
why: Removes existing scale; chemicals need careful handling.

text: Shut in and clean or replace the choke trim.
why: Definitive fix, but needs a short shutdown.

text: Open the choke further to compensate.
why: Keeps production short-term while deposits keep growing.

not_when.reason: The choke is already fully open.

text: Depressurize the line slowly from BOTH sides of the plug, then let the hydrate dissociate.
why: PetroWiki: two-sided depressurization is the recommended, safer method; it can take days.

text: Bring coiled tubing to place inhibitor (MEG/methanol) at the plug face.
why: Works where inhibitor cannot reach the plug otherwise; needs a vessel (> US$500k/day).

text: Increase hydrate-inhibitor dosing while the line still flows.
why: Best in the early stage, before the line is fully blocked.

not_when.reason: Flow has stopped, so the plug has formed; PetroWiki: inhibitor injection is usually ineffective because it cannot reach the plug face.

text: Depressurize from one side only to clear the plug faster.
why: Faster, but the plug can shoot down the line like a projectile.

text: Heat the line at the middle of the plug.
why: Gas released inside the plug can be trapped and burst the pipe.

text: Depressurize the service line from both sides and inject inhibitor.
why: Same principle as for the production line: two-sided depressurization is safer.

text: Stop gas lift through the blocked line and produce without it meanwhile.
why: Avoids pushing gas against the plug; production may fall.

text: Raise gas-lift pressure to blow the plug through.
why: Builds a pressure difference across the plug — projectile risk, and can compact the plug.

text: Schedule a downhole-gauge check; until fixed, base decisions on TPT and choke sensors.
why: The thesis notes PDGs commonly fail or freeze.

text: Schedule a subsea transducer (TPT) check.
why: TPT is one of the most important sensors for diagnosis.
